title: Meridian telemetry POC - queue drain & cost sampler
body:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures the Meridian (telemetry vendor) POC where we evaluated queue-drain behavior, tail-latency under intermittent microbursts, and the unit-cost tradeoffs across model variants and routing policies. Goal is to produce actionable config recommendations for a customer-grade deployment (Dedicated pool) and a fallback policy for Hosted usage.

High-level test goals:
- Reproduce customer-like mixed workload: 60% short chat-style queries (~30 tokens out), 30% mid-size summarization (~200 tokens out), 10% long synthesis (~800 tokens out).
- Inject periodic microbursts (30s spikes) to stress autoscaler and observe queue drain after spikes end.
- Compare two routing policies: latency-first (route to larger GPU with smaller batch latency SLO) vs cost-first (route to quantized variants on cheaper instances).
- Measure p50/p95/p99 generation latency, sustained throughput, GPU utilization, and estimated cost per 100k tokens.

Test harness and workload generator:
- Load generator: custom harness (bench-runner v0.9). Workload script: workloads/meridian_mixed_profile.yaml (open PR linked).
- Spike schedule: every 10 minutes, ramp 0 -> 300 RPS in 6s, hold 30s, ramp down in 10s. Baseline sustained rate 40 RPS.
- Session affinity: none (stateless requests).
- KV/cache warmup: tests ran both cold (new pod pool) and warm (30-minute warmup period).

Environment and infra:
- Deployment targets: Redwood Dedicated (eu-west-1 cluster) and Hosted API region eu-west-1 for comparison.
- Dedicated pool config: 6x H100-80GB nodes, 3 initial pods (autoscale min=2,max=12), instance type: h100-dedicated, model pinned per route.
- Hosted run: default routing, no reserved capacity, Redwood-managed pool.
- Autoscaler policy observed: scale-up threshold at 70% GPU utilization sustained for 20s, scale-down after 6m idle.

Model variants tested:
- meridian-gpt-small-q4_0 (quantized 4-bit, 8GB KV footprint) - cost-first candidate
- meridian-gpt-medium-fp16 (fp16, 24GB KV) - balanced candidate
- meridian-gpt-large-8bit (8-bit, 48GB KV) - latency-first candidate for heavy workloads

Batching and request settings:
- baseline batching: max_batch_tokens=2048, max_batch_size=32, batch_window_ms=8
- aggressive batching trial: max_batch_tokens=8192, max_batch_size=64, batch_window_ms=12 (for cost-first runs)
- prefix caching: enabled for warm runs only; prefix cache hit rate measured separately

Key observations (quantitative):
Note: numbers are aggregated over three 1-hour runs (cold, warm, tuned). Token counts normalized to generated tokens only (not input tokens).

1) Dedicated, latency-first routing (meridian-gpt-large-8bit, H100 pool, baseline batching, warm):
- sustained throughput (steady state): 420 qps (short queries), mixed-workload steady effective throughput ~185 qps
- p50 latency: 28 ms (short), 120 ms (mid), 540 ms (long)
- p95 latency: 140 ms (short), 560 ms (mid), 2.2 s (long)
- p99 latency: 420 ms (short), 1.9 s (mid), 6.8 s (long)
- GPU utilization: 78% average during sustained periods, spikes to 96% during bursts
- Observed queue drain: after burst ends, p99 spikes up to 3x baseline for 40-70s due to queue reordering and NVMe cache thrash on some nodes
- Estimated cost: $42 per 100k generated tokens (model compute only, excluding infra baseline)

2) Dedicated, cost-first routing (meridian-gpt-small-q4_0 on cheaper nodes, aggressive batching):
- sustained throughput: 310 qps steady (short), mixed-workload effective throughput ~140 qps
- p50 latency: 62 ms (short), 340 ms (mid), 1.6 s (long)
- p95 latency: 400 ms (short), 1.6 s (mid), 5.2 s (long)
- p99 latency: 1.3 s (short), 4.6 s (mid), 12.1 s (long)
- GPU utilization: 55% avg, with higher CPU-side batching overhead observed
- Queue drain: longer tail post-burst (p99 elevated for 120-180s) driven by cold KV/cache misses and larger aggregated batches causing queuing behind long-running requests
- Estimated cost: $11 per 100k generated tokens (model compute only)

3) Hosted baseline (mixed routing by Redwood):
- sustained throughput: 365 qps steady (mix)
- tail latency behavior sits between Dedicated-latency-first and cost-first
- p99 spikes on hosted were lower amplitude and shorter duration than dedicated-cost-first, thanks to automatic fallback to higher-tier pools in the control plane during sustained high contention
- Observed difference: hosted smoothing plus multi-pool routing reduces extreme queue drain but increases average cost compared to Dedicated cost-first

Cold vs warm behavior:
- Cold runs show pronounced p99 spikes across all variants after bursts (p99 2-3x warm-run p99). Cause: cache misses for prefetched KV and model memory pages, plus node scaling events that create short window of constrained capacity.
- Warm runs with prefix cache warmed to >65% hit rate saw p99 cut by ~35% for mid/long requests compared to cold.

Root cause analysis for queue-drain tail spikes:
- Primary contributors: (1) burst-induced long-running generation jobs accumulating; (2) autoscaler scale-down policy and pod churn causing short-lived capacity gaps; (3) batch accumulation across requests of heterogeneous size (long requests block queues for short ones when batching is aggressive); (4) cache eviction policy (NVMe-backed KV cache) thrash during sudden load shifts.

Customer-facing recommendations (config & architectural):
1) Keep a small warm buffer: set min_pods = ceil(expected_peak_qps / single_pod_peak_qps) + 1 for Dedicated pools handling spiky telemetry workloads. For Meridian this maps to min=4 (we used 3 and saw drain).
2) Autoscaler tweak: shorten scale-up to 8–12s (from 20s) and lengthen scale-down to 8–10m to avoid scale oscillation that coincides with periodic spikes.
3) Routing policy: enable hybrid routing—prefer latency-first for short interactive routes and cost-first for background batch jobs. Add request hints (latency_required=true/false) from the app.
4) Batch configuration: enforce batch_priority queueing—small/short responses prioritized for dispatch into small batches while long/gen jobs scheduled into separate batch lane to avoid head-of-line blocking. Max_batch_size=24 for mix; long lane can use 64.
5) Prefix/KV cache: require warmup during deployment windows; set cache-reserve on a fraction of nodes to avoid complete eviction during bursts.
6) Eviction settings: move to LRU with size-aware heuristics; limit per-request persistent KV usage or cap per-session memory to prevent a few large sessions from causing eviction cascades.
7) Cost-control guardrails: for cost-sensitive customers, add policy that automatically routes <=10% of traffic to latency-first pools during sustained >80% utilization windows to bound p99 without blowing cost.

Operational playbook (quick runbook for SRE/SE):
- Pre-deployment: run 30m warmup job (workloads/meridian_warmup.yaml).
- If p99 > Service SLO during business hours: increase min_pods by 1, reduce batch_window_ms by 2ms for short-lane.
- If cost > budget: enable cost-first route for non-critical endpoints and rerun cost estimation after 2 hours.

Follow-ups and action items:
- SE-4217: implement lane-based batching POC in serving runtime (owner: Liam) — target spike window simulation by 2028-11-15.
- PR bench-playbooks#138: add warmup and cache monitoring hooks (owner: Sofia) — merge by 2028-11-08.
- Customer proposal: draft a Dedicated pool config with min=4,max=12, routing rules, and estimated 12-month cost model (owner: Priya) — deliver to Meridian by 2028-11-06.
- SRE ask: evaluate autoscaler sensitivity tests (scale-up 8/12/20s) in lower env and report stable config (owner: Ravi) — 2028-11-12.

Notes / informal observations:
- We saw one node with kernel-level page cache stalls during long repeated heavy long-gen runs; SRE will open infra ticket to inspect node NVMe health (ticket linked in SE-4217).
- Meridian engineering is open to shipping hints (latency_required) from their edge aggregator which will make hybrid routing very effective.
- On-hosted runs, Redwood control plane smoothed some of the worst tails — this is a defensible story for customers who value simplicity over minimizing marginal token cost.

Appendix: quick numbers snapshot (warm runs, mixed workload, baseline batching)
- meridian-gpt-large-8bit: p50/p95/p99 = 120ms / 2.2s / 6.8s, cost = $42/100k tokens
- meridian-gpt-medium-fp16: p50/p95/p99 = 220ms / 1.9s / 5.4s, cost = $23/100k tokens
- meridian-gpt-small-q4_0: p50/p95/p99 = 62ms / 400ms / 1.3s, cost = $11/100k tokens

Concluding summary:
Meridian's mixed telemetry workload shows a clear tradeoff between minimizing token cost and bounding tail latency. For production SLAs the immediate wins are operational: keep a small warm buffer, apply lane-based batching to avoid head-of-line blocking, and tune autoscaler (faster scale-up, slower scale-down). For customers most sensitive to unit cost, offer a documented fallback and alerting policy that allows short bursts to degrade gracefully into cost-first modes while keeping critical interactive routes on latency-first pools.

If reviewers want raw logs, perf traces, and the bench-runner config, see linked artifacts above and bench artifacts in PR (#138).
